title: Part 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text: Extension of simple linear regression to more than one (continuous/ordinal) independent variables.

title: Part 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Assumptions

Level of measurement
Sample size
Linearity between outcome and predictors
Independence of observations
Homoscedasticity of residuals
Normality of residuals
No multicollinearity
No extreme outliers
No overfitting

title: Part 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Level of Measurement & Sample size

Level of measurement:

Dependent variable: Continuous.
Independent variables: Continuous or dichotomous.

Sample size: n = #subjects, m = #independant var:

Should be at least 10 or 20 times as many observations as there are independent variables (\(n>>m\)) otherwise the estimates of the regression are unstable.

Linearity between outcome and predictors:

Look at the plot of residuals vs. predicted values.
If the residuals are spread randomly around a straight line, this suggests that the assumption that the relationship is linear is reasonable.

Independence of observations:

Each observation in the data set corresponds to a different individual.
Look at the plot of residuals vs. predicted values.
If the residuals are spread randomly around the residual = 0 line, this suggests that the assumption of independence of observations is reasonable.

Homoscedasticity of residuals:

Look at the plot of residuals vs. predicted values.
If size of errors proportional to size of predictors, can be due to violation of linearity and/or independence of errors.
Solution: log-transformation of the dependent variable.

Normality of residuals:

Look at the residuals normal probability plot.
Points should fall close to the diagonal line.
If not, can be due to variables non-normally distributed, non-linear relationship, outliers, etc.
Solution: log-transformation of the variables.

No Multicollinearity:

If two independent variables are closely related (correlation coefficient is high) it is difficult to estimate their regression coefficients because they tend to get confused and they will cancel each other out and destroy the model.
This difficulty is called collinearity.
Solution is to exclude one of the highly correlated variables.

Outliers:

Outliers can have a strong influence on the regression estimates.
Solution depends on the origin of the outlier.

title: Part 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Overfitting:
In multivariable modeling, you can get highly significant but meaningless results if you put too many predictors in the model compared to the number of samples.
The model is fit perfectly to the quirks of your particular sample but has no predictive ability in a new sample.
A common approach that controls over fitting by keeping the number of predictors to a minimum is stepwise multiple regression:

Start with the one predictor that explains the most predicted variance (i.e., has the highest correlation coefficient with the outcome).
Statistically significant predictors are added to the model one at a time.
The process is repeated until no remaining predictor has a statistically significant correlation with the outcome.

title: Part 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Coefficient of determination (\(R^2\))
\(R^2\):

Represents the proportion of the dependent variable explained by combined effects of the independent variables.
Indicates how well the model fits the data.

\(R^2_{adjusted}\):

Used for estimating explained variance in a population (\(≠\) sample).
Used when sample size is small and when results have to be generalized.
Corrects for overparameterization.

title: Part 3: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Non-linear models

Linear Regression fits a straight line to your data.
Non-linear models may, in some cases, be more appropriate.
Non-linear models are usually used when non-linear relationships have some biological explanation. (e.g. non-linear models are commonly used in compartmental analysis).

Run analysis with transformed beta-plasma (logbetaplasma).

From the top menu, select Plots > Histogram.
Move betaplasma into Variable and check Show Density.



Reminder
Sometimes data are non-normally distributed but closely related log-normally distributed.


Distribution right-skewed
The logarithm of the data is thus normal

The log-transformation of data is very common, mostly to eliminate skewness in data.

Other kinds of normalization:

When data are counts: square-root transformation

\(x_{transf} = \sqrt{x + 1/2}\)

When data are proportions: arcsine transformation

\(x_{transf} = arcsin(\sqrt{x})\)

When data are frequency distribution of data is left-skewed: square transformation

\(x_{transf} = x^2\)

title: Part 1: Correlation
text:
Two quantitative measurements can be related.
They are called the dependent variable (\(Y\)) and the independent variable (\(X\)).

Q How can you describe the relationship between two numerical variables?

Correlation: Describes the degree of association between variables.
Regression: Describes the effect of variable \(X\) on variable \(Y\).




A correlation measures the “degree of association” between two variables.
Associations can be:

Positive: An increase in one variable is associated with an increase in the other.
Negative: An increase in one variable is associated with a decrease in the other.





To measure the “degree of association” between:

2 continuous variables (normally distributed) –> Pearson’s correlation coefficient
2 continuous variables (non normally distributed) –> Spearman’s rank
2 categorical variables (ordinal) –> Kendall’s Tau







WarningReminder



Normality of variables is tested using the Shapiro-Wilk test: Ho:variable normally distributed





The Pearson’s correlation coefficient is defined as:
\[r = \frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})(y - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 \sum (y - \bar{y})^2}}\]
It describes how \(Y\) varies with \(X\) (numerator):
\(-1 \leq r \leq 1\)
\(r = -1\) # 100% negative correlation \(r = 1\) # 100% positive correlation






Value
Interpretation




\(r = 0\)
no relationship


\(\lvert r \rvert = 1\)
perfect linear relationship


\(\lvert r \rvert < 0.3\)
weak relationship


\(0.3 \leq \lvert r \rvert \leq 0.7\)
moderate relationship


\(\lvert r \rvert > 0.7\)
strong relationship



The p-value assigned to \(r\) tells us how likely \(r\) is right (i.e., confidence in our statement).



Pearson’s \(r\) can be squared, \(r^2\), to derive a coefficient of determination.
It explains the portion of variability in one of the variables that can be accounted for by the variability in the second one.
Example: Correlation between 2 variables \(X\) and \(Y\)
Pearson’s coefficient: \(r\) = -0.7 –> \(r^2\) = 0.49
49% of the variability in variable \(X\) is determined by the variability of variable \(Y\).



Scatter-plot

Displays the relationship between 2 continuous variables.
Each point represents the paired value of the variables for each individual.
Useful in the early stage of analysis when exploring data and determining if a linear regression analysis is appropriate.

title: Part 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
In correlation, the two variables are treated as equals.
In regression, one variable is considered as:

Independent variable \(X\) (predictor)
Dependent variable \(Y\) (outcome)



Regression analysis is used to describe the relationship between:
A single outcome variable: \(y\), and One or more predictor variables: \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k\)

If \(k = 1\) : Simple linear regression
If \(k > 1\) : Multiple linear regression

Predicting \(Y\) based on a given value of \(X\)
\(X\) = Independent / Predictor variable (continuous, categorical or nominal)
\(Y\) = Dependent / Outcome variable (continuous)
\[
y = a + bx + e
\]
where:

\(y\) = the observed value of the outcome variable
\(a\) = the intercept
\(b\) = the regression coefficient (slope)
\(x\) = the value of the predictor variable
\(e\) = the error or residual

Test of significance: \(b\) is significantly different from zero

Problem: To draw a straight line through the points that best explains the relationship.










Line can then be used to predict \(Y\) from \(X\).



A good line is the one that minimises the sum of squared differences between the points and the line.
The smaller the sum of squared differences, the better the fit of the line to the data.
Sum of squared differences:
Green line:
(1-4.5)^2 +(4-4.5)^2 + (4-4.5)^2 + (7-4.5)^2 +(8-4.5)^2 = 31.25
Blue line:
(1-2)^2 + (4-3)^2 + (4-4.5)^2 + (7-6)^2 + (8-7.5)^2 = 3.5




Using calculus, we get:
\[
b =
\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}
     {\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
=
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)}
     {\operatorname{Var}(x)}
\]
\[
a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}
\]
Coefficient \(b\) is related to the correlation coefficient \(r\).
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are positively correlated, then slope \(b\) is positive.
\[
r = b\frac{SD_x}{SD_y}
\]



Is the slope significantly different from zero?



Hypothesis
\(H_0: b = 0\) (no relationship)



\(H_1: b ≠ 0\) (linear relationship)


Test of significance
\(T = b/SE(b)\)


Result
p-value significant or not


Conclusion
the slope is different from zero



significant linear relationship







The residual for observation \(i(e_i)\) is the difference between its observed and predicted value:

\(e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}i\)

Check the assumptions of regression by examining the residuals
Examine for linearity assumption
Examine for constant variance for all levels of \(X\) (homoscedasticity)
Evaluate normal distribution assumption
Evaluate independence assumption
Check the presence of outliers




\(R^2\)

Represents the proportion of the dependent variable explained by the independent variable.
Indicates how well the model fits the data.

\(R^2_{adjusted}\)

Used for estimating explained variance in a population (\(≠\) sample).
Used when sample size is small and when results have to be generalized.

Linear regression equation:
\[

\]







Term
Meaning




\(\hat{Y}\)
Predicted value: predicted value of \(Y\)


\(a\)
Intercept: value of \(Y\) when \(X = 0\)


\(b\)
Slope: predicted change in \(Y\) for each one-unit increase in \(X\)

title: Part 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Linear regression equation:
\[
CHD_{pred} = a + b * Cig. cons
\]







Term
Meaning




CHD_{pred}
Predicted value: predicted value of CHD


\(a\)
Intercept: level of CHD when zero Cig is consumed


\(b\)
Slope: rate of increase of CHD for each unit increase of Cig consumption

title: Part 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Regression coefficients:

p-value < 0.05 means \(b\) is significantly different from zero.
There is a significant linear relationship between Cig consumption and CHD mortality.

title: Part 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Regression model:
\[
\hat{Y} = a + bX = 2.37 + 2.04X
\]

“CHD mortality” is equal to 2.37 when zero cigarette is consumed.
“CHD mortality” is increased by 2.04 units per increase of “Cig consumption” units.

title: Part 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Prediction:
What is the “CHD mortality” when cigarette consumption is 6?
\[
\hat{Y} = a + bX = 2.37 + 2.04(6) = 14.61
\]
We predict 14.61 / 10,000 people will die of CHD per annum in a country with an average consumption of 6 cigarettes per adult.

title: Part 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Accuracy of prediction (residuals):
Residuals are the vertical distance between actual and predicted values.

\(X = 6\) cigarettes per adult per day
Prediction: 14.61 deaths / 10,000
What they actually have: 23 deaths / 10,000
Residual error for this case: 23 - 14.61 = 8.39
Explained variance:
\(r = 0.71\)
\(r^2 = 0.71^2 = 0.51\)
Conclusion: Almost 50% in variability of incidence of CHD mortality is associated with variability in smoking rates.

title: Part 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Model Summary
Model Fit Measures:

\(R\): Pearson Correlation Coefficient between Age and Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) of 0.315.
\(R^2_{adjusted}\): Coefficient of determination of 0.09, meaning that Age accounts for ~ 9% of the variation of SBP.


ANOVA Test:

\(p\): Significance level associated to F-ratio. It is < 0.05. Meaning that the regression model predicts SBP significantly well.


Model Coefficients:

Predictor: Estimations of model parameters – Intersect(\(a\)) and Slope Coefficient (\(b\)).

Age has a significant effect on SBP (\(p < 0.05\)). For one year increase in age there was 0.604 unit increase in SBP level.

95% C.I. for \(b\): SBP level increases by between 0.24 and 0.97 mmHg by one year increase in age.

title: Part 2: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Confidence and prediction

Confidence intervals tell how well you have determined the estimate parameter. The standard error for a CI takes into account the uncertainty due to sampling.
Prediction intervals tell where you can expect to see the next data point sampled (give a range for \(y\) itself). The standard error for a PI takes into account the uncertainty due to sampling + the variability of the individuals around the predicted mean.
Both intervals will be centered around the same value, but the standard errors will be different. A prediction interval is always wider than a confidence interval.

Residual analysis for Homoscedasticity

Residual analysis for Independence of observations

No extreme outliers
Cases with extreme values that differ greatly from the rest of your sample.

Even a few outliers can dramatically change estimates of the slope (\(b\)).


Outliers can result from:

Errors in coding or data entry (→ rectify).
Impossible values in real life (→ exclude).
Or sometimes they reflect important “real” variation (→ include, run the analysis both with and without it).

If you see no reason why your outliers are erroneous measurements → there is no truly objective way to remove them.
